comment: Leading with bevacizumab puts the smallest effect on the board at rank 1: GOG-218 is PFS-only at HR 0.717 (pmid:22204724) with no overall-population OS gain, while the all-comer PARP options sit at HR 0.62 and HR 0.52 and PAOLA-1 reaches HR 0.33 if the GIS clears 42 (pmid:31851799). She is already on the bevacizumab backbone, so ranking it first spends nothing new and forfeits the larger maintenance signal. For a tumor that is BRCA-wild-type but genomically unstable, the right move is to force the GIS question, not bank the safe PFS curve.

Her stated efficacy_toxicity_weight is 0.7, and leading with bevacizumab fits the tolerability half while leaving the efficacy half on the table: GOG-218 gives PFS-only HR 0.717 (pmid:22204724) against an all-comer niraparib HR 0.62 and a PAOLA-1 HRD-positive HR 0.33 (pmid:31851799). The veto she named is severe myelosuppression, not the PARP class itself, so the path that honors a 0.7 lean is a hematology-supported niraparib dose plan or the GIS that opens olaparib + bevacizumab, not the curve she is already riding. I would not seat the lowest-magnitude maintenance at rank 1 for a patient who weighted efficacy above tolerability.

The pick is right and the all-comer PRIMA enrollment is the clean eligibility match (pmid:31562799), so I am with the critic on niraparib. Where I push back: setting expectations strictly off the all-comer HR 0.62 ignores tumor-specific pharmacology that points niraparib at exactly this BRCA-proficient biology, where it partitioned into tumor at 3.3x plasma and cut growth 58% in a BRCA-wild-type PDX that olaparib barely touched (pmid:30647846). That preclinical signal is thin evidence, but it argues the upside here runs above the registration-population number rather than at it.

Anchoring rank 1 to the NCCN category 2A all-comer status of niraparib (pmid:31562799) quietly demotes the one regimen with the largest effect on the board, PAOLA-1 olaparib + bevacizumab at HRD-positive HR 0.33 (pmid:31851799), to a contingent second place. She is already on the bevacizumab half and the only gate is a single MyChoice GIS that runs on archival FFPE, so the guideline-clean default understates how cheaply the high-magnitude option could open. I would order the GIS and treat that combination as the lead pending the score, not slot the all-comer agent first because it carries no contingency.

I am vetoing this rank-1 pick on toxicity grounds. PAOLA-1 (pmid:31851799) runs combination-arm grade 3+ AE near 57% with grade 3+ hypertension 19%, and stacking that anti-angiogenic bleeding/VTE load onto a patient whose preferences.json modality_constraints flag high VTE history and a prior IVC filter has no compensating safety-mitigation evidence in the record. The veto lifts only if a documented anticoagulation/BP-management plan accompanies a confirmed MyChoice GIS at least 42; absent the score she is not even eligible and the HR 0.33 never reaches her.

I veto niraparib at rank 1 on the patient's own severe-myelosuppression / febrile-neutropenia veto in preferences.json. PRIMA (pmid:31562799) reports grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7% and anemia 31%, and her baseline WBC of 3.5 leaves thin marrow reserve in the 70-79 band, so individualized starting dose blunts but does not erase the hazard. The veto is conditional: I will withdraw it only once a hematology-supported dose plan and a written cytopenia-management pathway are on file, at which point niraparib is a reasonable all-comer choice.

The guideline read is sound (NCCN 2A all-comer PARP per PRIMA pmid:31562799), and I credit you for naming the myelosuppression veto rather than burying it. My qualification is the confidence:high label: with grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7% and anemia 31% landing on her stated veto and a baseline WBC of 3.5, the toxicity-gated confidence in this specific patient should sit lower until a platelet-based starting dose and counts pathway are documented. Guideline fit is high; deliverability at her marrow reserve is not yet established.

I endorse leading with bevacizumab on safety-characterization grounds. It is the one maintenance axis whose toxicity I can predict: FDA-approved since 2014, GOG-218 (pmid:22204724) grade 2+ hypertension 22.9% vs 7.2% with a well-worn management algorithm and bowel-wall disruption held at 2.6%, and it clears both named vetoes in preferences.json. My one caution matches yours: the VTE/bleeding risk against her IVC-filter history needs the established BP and bleeding monitoring kept running rather than escalated, but that is a managed caution, not a veto trigger.

The entire rank-1 case rests on the PAOLA-1 HRD-positive subgroup HR 0.33, but the pre-specified ITT was HR 0.59 (0.49-0.72) and the ITT OS was not significant, so the headline 66% vs 48% 5-year OS is a subgroup readout (pmid:31851799). She has no validated GIS, so she does not even clear the companion-diagnostic gate that defines that subgroup. Ranking a not-yet-eligible patient first off a subgroup estimate, with the gating assay still pending, is the case the veto exists for.

Ranking the agent she already tolerates first is defensible, and GOG-218 (pmid:22204724) is the one RoB2-low row in the set. My qualifier is the survival framing: both GOG-218 and ICON7 are PFS-only with no ITT OS benefit (PFS HR 0.717), and the ICON7 survival signal sits in the open-label high-risk subgroup, not the ITT. Keep the pick, but label it a PFS hold, not a survival argument.

You rank rucaparib on ATHENA-MONO, and the all-comer ITT footing is the right read for a BRCA wild-type tumor, and the estimand is settled at ITT HR 0.52 (95% CI 0.40-0.68) from the primary JCO publication (pmid:35658487). My residual point is that rucaparib is the redundant second all-comer PARP, so ranking it ahead of niraparib rests on board-agreement arithmetic rather than a distinct biological edge.

Ranking letrozole second reads it almost entirely off preference_fit, where it does clear her vetoes. On evidence it is the weakest pick on your list: pmid:29157627 is a single non-randomized cohort, ROBINS-I Serious, n=80, 60% vs 38.5% recurrence-free at 24 months, and her PR-negativity tempers even that. Rank it for preference if you must, but the ROBINS-I Serious tag belongs next to the rank, not buried in the concerns where a reader takes the 60% for a trial result.

NCCN Ovarian v1.2025 ranks PAOLA-1 olaparib plus bevacizumab as category 1, but only for HRD-positive disease defined by tumor BRCA or a validated GIS at or above 42 (pmid:31851799). Leading with this regimen ahead of the MyChoice CDx result puts a category-1 indication on a patient who is not yet in its endorsed population, and the Altera qualitative instability call does not clear that companion-diagnostic bar. Force the assay first, as the board agrees; until it reads at or above 42 the guideline-aligned choice is all-comer niraparib, not the gated combination.

Putting bevacizumab first is consistent with NCCN Ovarian v1.2025, which lists bevacizumab maintenance as a category 2A all-comer option after 1L platinum, anchored by GOG-218 and ICON7 (pmid:22204724). My one qualifier: the same guideline places single-agent PARP maintenance at category 2A for all-comers too, and PRIMA needs no validated HRD score (pmid:31562799), so ranking niraparib below bevacizumab is a tolerability call rather than a guideline-tier one. Both are 2A, so name the trade-off as toxicity versus a larger PFS effect, not as one regimen having stronger guideline standing.

The critic demotes PAOLA-1 to rank 3 as a subgroup-gated estimate, and on RoB grounds that is fair, but NCCN Ovarian v1.2025 still carries this regimen at category 1 for HRD-positive disease, which is the panel's calibration of that same predefined HRD-positive analysis, not a stratum the guideline treats as exploratory (pmid:31851799). The real constraint is eligibility, not evidence quality: the indication is gated on a validated GIS at or above 42 the patient does not yet have. We agree on the conclusion for now, but the regimen's guideline tier should not be talked down once the MyChoice CDx confirms HRD-positive.

Letrozole has a place in NCCN Ovarian v1.2025, which includes aromatase inhibitors among hormone-therapy options, and her roughly 80 percent ER-positive staining supports it, so I do not dissent on fit. The qualifier is the tier: endocrine therapy here rests on a non-randomized retrospective series (pmid:29157627, ROBINS-I serious) and sits at a softer recommendation than the category 2A PARP and bevacizumab options, and her PR-negativity predicts a tempered response. Frame it as the low-toxicity later-line or adjunct fallback if the GIS returns HRD-negative, not as a maintenance option carrying the same guideline weight as the ranked PARP and anti-angiogenic choices.

Leading with PAOLA-1 olaparib + bevacizumab (pmid:31851799) puts her highest-burden option first, and it stacks both things she asked us to weigh against: the combination-arm grade 3+ myelosuppression sits on her severe-myelosuppression veto, and the bevacizumab half presses her thrombotic/bleeding caution given the VTE history and prior IVC filter. Forcing the GIS to chase the HR 0.43 subgroup is a reasonable workup, but ranking the regimen itself at the top of an efficacy_toxicity_weight 0.7 patient who folded tolerability in is the wrong order for her. Send the MyChoice score, hold the combination as conditional below the rank she gave it.

This is the pick I lead with too, and for the same patient-side reason: bevacizumab (pmid:22204724) is the only maintenance on the board that clears both named vetoes, no added neuropathy and no severe myelosuppression, on a backbone she already tolerates. The VTE and bleeding caution you flag against her high VTE history and prior IVC filter is exactly the modality_constraint that needs active monitoring rather than escalation. The PFS-only ceiling is the honest tradeoff, and for a woman in the 70-79 band who weighted tolerability into a 0.7 lean, a regimen she tolerates beats a stronger one that trips a veto.

Your evidence read on PRIMA (pmid:31562799) is the strongest on the board and I do not contest it, but ranking niraparib first runs straight into the patient's severe-myelosuppression veto: grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7% and anemia 31%, on a baseline WBC already at 3.5. Individualized starting dose blunts that, it does not clear the veto, and the veto is hers to lift, not ours to rank past on evidence grounds. I would not put a veto-tripping agent at rank 1 for her unless she chose to accept that risk with hematology support documented first.

Niraparib is the cleanest guideline fit, agreed, but guideline-clean is not preference-clean here: PRIMA grade 3+ thrombocytopenia 28.7% and anemia 31% (pmid:31562799) land directly on her severe-myelosuppression veto, and the oral route you credit does not offset a toxicity she explicitly named as a stop. The category 2A all-comer footing earns it a place on the list, not rank 1 for this patient. I would slot it behind the options that clear both vetoes and document a cytopenia-management plan before offering it as the lead.
